## Background

A risk analyst at a private wealth manager wants to compute the range of potential outcomes for a client's retirement portfolio.  

::: {.callout-caution title="Question"}
How might the analyst use Generative models like Gaussian parametric, nonparametric kernel density, and a GAN?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The analyst needs to forecast returns.  Unlike point forecasts, we need a probabilistic range of forecasts.  One approach is to use a Generative Model; i.e. a model that generates realistic simulations of the return process.  By stringing together several days' returns we can simulate how the initial client's wealth could evolve through time.  By repeating that process over many simulated paths, we create a range of outcomes that can be used to assess the risk embedded within the client's portfolio. 

Three Generative Models are i) parameteric density fitting, wherein we choose a distributional form (e.g. Gaussian) wherein we fit that form to the data, and then simulate from the estimated density, ii) Kernel Density estimation, which is a non parametric approach that uses the empirical distribution of the data to form a simulator, and iii) a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), which trains a neural network generator to produce simulated returns that a second neural network (the discriminator) cannot distinguish from historical returns.
:::




## Housekeeping

```{r}
#| label: setup

cat("\014")  # clear console
rm(list=ls())  # Clear the workspace

required_packages <- c("tidyverse", "scales", "knitr", "keras3")
missing_packages <- required_packages[!vapply(required_packages, requireNamespace,
                                               quietly = TRUE, FUN.VALUE = logical(1))]
if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  stop("Install these packages before rendering: ", paste(missing_packages, collapse = ", "))
}

library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(here)

# Pin the Python virtualenv created by keras3::install_keras() explicitly.
# Without this, reticulate's automatic environment discovery can behave
# inconsistently depending on how R was launched (e.g. via Positron vs. a
# shell), and in some contexts attempts to provision an unrelated ephemeral
# environment instead of reusing the one already configured for keras3.
reticulate_venv <- file.path(Sys.getenv("USERPROFILE"), "Documents", ".virtualenvs", "r-keras")
if (dir.exists(reticulate_venv)) {
  reticulate::use_virtualenv(reticulate_venv, required = TRUE)
}
library(keras3)

source(here("Topics/Generative", "ReturnSimulation-Helpers.R"))

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.title.position = "plot"
    )
)

set.seed(20260905)
keras3::set_random_seed(20260905)

# Simulation settings. These are fixed constants; the exercise is small enough
# that the full run completes quickly.
N_PATHS <- 1000L
SIMULATION_DAYS <- 252L
ONE_DAY_DRAWS <- 100000L
KDE_QUANTILE_DRAWS <- 20000L

# GAN settings. Kept small and trained for few epochs so that a GAN is fit
# separately for each of the four assets without materially slowing down
# rendering. See the "GAN model" section for what each setting controls.
GAN_Z_DIM <- 32L
GAN_HIDDEN_UNITS <- 64L
GAN_EPOCHS <- 50L
GAN_BATCH_SIZE <- 32L
GAN_LEARNING_RATE <- 2e-4

model_colors <- c(
  "Historical" = "grey35",
  "Gaussian" = "#0072B2",
  "KDE" = "#D55E00",
  "GAN" = "#009E73"
)

asset_levels <- c("Asset 1", "Asset 2", "Asset 3", "Asset 4")
```

`N_PATHS` is the number of simulated one-year paths per asset and model.
`ONE_DAY_DRAWS` is the size of the large one-day sample used to compare fitted
marginal distributions. `KDE_QUANTILE_DRAWS` controls the reference sample used
for KDE interval and tail quantiles during validation.

## Data

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
Load the simulated returns. The returns were generated by
[`SimulatedData-ReturnDistributions.R`](SimulatedData-ReturnDistributions.R)
and stored in `data/KDE-returns.csv`. 
::: 


```{r}
#| label: load-data

asset_returns <- read_csv(here("data", "KDE-returns.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(date),
    asset_id = factor(asset_id, levels = asset_levels)
  )

sample_check <- asset_returns |>
  summarise(
    assets = n_distinct(asset_id),
    trading_days = n_distinct(date),
    observations = n(),
    first_date = min(date),
    last_date = max(date),
    missing_returns = sum(is.na(return)),
    minimum_observations_per_asset = min(table(asset_id)),
    maximum_observations_per_asset = max(table(asset_id))
  )
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(sample_check, caption = "Synthetic sample integrity checks")
```
:::

The dates are synthetic weekday labels. Exchange holidays are intentionally
outside the scope of the lesson.

### Calibration and validation samples

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
Use the first four years to fit the models and reserve the fifth year for
validation.
:::

```{r}
#| label: split-sample

all_dates <- sort(unique(asset_returns$date))
calibration_dates <- all_dates[1:1008]
validation_dates <- all_dates[1009:1260]

calibration <- asset_returns |>
  filter(date %in% calibration_dates)

validation <- asset_returns |>
  filter(date %in% validation_dates)

split_check <- bind_rows(
  calibration |> summarise(sample = "Calibration", start = min(date), end = max(date),
                           days = n_distinct(date), observations = n()),
  validation |> summarise(sample = "Validation", start = min(date), end = max(date),
                          days = n_distinct(date), observations = n())
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}
```{r}
#| echo = FALSE
kable(split_check, caption = "Chronological calibration and validation samples")
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
Why should we not evaluate the models only on the data used to fit them?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- A flexible model can look especially accurate in sample because it adapts
  closely to the calibration observations.
- Strong in-sample fit does not guarantee that the model will describe new
  returns well.
- A later validation period tests whether the fitted distribution generalizes.
- The validation observations must not influence parameter or bandwidth
  estimation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
Which features would make a Gaussian model potentially inadequate?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- substantial skewness;
- tails heavier than those of a Gaussian distribution;
- systematic tail deviations from the reference line in a Gaussian Q–Q plot;
- multiple modes or mixture-like features; and
- extreme losses that occur more frequently than a fitted Gaussian predicts.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
For each asset, recommend the Gaussian model, KDE, or a GAN. Justify the
recommendation using the histogram, Q–Q plot, skewness, kurtosis, and tail
quantiles.
:::

## Gaussian parametric model

### Estimation

For asset $i$, estimate the calibration-period mean and standard deviation:

$$
\widehat{\mu}_i=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{it},
\qquad
\widehat{\sigma}_i=
\sqrt{\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(r_{it}-\widehat{\mu}_i)^2}.
$$

The fitted model assumes:

$$
r_{i,t}^{\mathrm{sim}}\sim N\left(\widehat{\mu}_i,\widehat{\sigma}_i^2\right).
$$

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
Summarize returns from the calibration set. 
:::

```{r}
#| label: fit-gaussian

gaussian_estimates <- calibration |>
  group_by(asset_id) |>
  summarise(
    mu = mean(return),
    sigma = sd(return),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```



::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(gaussian_estimates, digits = 5, caption = "Gaussian parameter estimates")
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
If the Gaussian simulation matches an asset's mean and standard deviation, does it reproduce the entire distribution?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- No. Matching the first two moments does not ensure that the model matches
  skewness, kurtosis, tail quantiles, or multiple modes.
- The Gaussian assumption imposes symmetry, zero excess kurtosis, and a
  particular relationship among all quantiles.
- The estimates also contain sampling error, even when the Gaussian assumption
  is correct.
:::

### Simulation

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
How can we use a Gaussian parametric simulation to achieve the risk manager's goal?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- Use each asset's calibration-period returns to estimate its mean and standard
  deviation.
- Assume future daily returns follow a Gaussian distribution with those
  estimated parameters.
- Draw many sequences of daily returns from the fitted distribution.
- Compound each sequence into a possible one-year wealth path.
- Summarize the paths using quantiles, loss probabilities, Value at Risk, and
  Expected Shortfall.
- The method is parametric because a small number of estimated parameters,
  together with the Gaussian assumption, determine the entire distribution.
:::

A single Gaussian draw for asset $i$ is simply $r^{\mathrm{sim}}=\widehat{\mu}_i
+\widehat{\sigma}_i\,z$ with $z\sim N(0,1)$. The helper `draw_gaussian()` returns
a vector of such draws.


::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
Create a temporary subset to focus on Asset 2
:::
```{r}
#| label: demonstrate-gaussian-draw
#| output: false

set.seed(4127)

gaussian_example <- gaussian_estimates |>
  filter(asset_id == "Asset 2")
tibble(simulated_return = draw_gaussian(10, gaussian_example$mu,
                                        gaussian_example$sigma)) |>
  mutate(simulated_return = percent(simulated_return, accuracy = 0.01)) |>
  kable(caption = "Ten illustrative Gaussian draws for Asset 2")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
tibble(simulated_return = draw_gaussian(10, gaussian_example$mu,
                                        gaussian_example$sigma)) |>
  mutate(simulated_return = percent(simulated_return, accuracy = 0.01)) |>
  kable(caption = "Ten illustrative Gaussian draws for Asset 2")
```
:::

## KDE model

### KDE Intuition

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
Can you describe the purpose and mechanics of KDE? 
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}

KDE is a nonparametric approach to simulation

- Parametric simulation:  assume a specific distribution (e.g., Gaussian), estimate a few parameters, and simulate from that assumed shape. 
- KDE simulation:  make no global distributional assumption; instead, approximate the density as a sum of small local densities centered at the observed data, then simulate from that empirical shape. 
- The Kernel density function is $\frac{1}{Th}\sum_{i=1}^{T}K(\frac{x-x_{i}}{h})$, where $N$  is the number of observations, $h>0$ is the smoothing parameter (aka bandwidth), and $K(.)$  is the kernel function, which integrates to 1. 
- Many Kernels are possible, such as Gaussian,  Uniform, Triangular, etc...

How KDE builds a smooth analogue of a histogram

1. Form empirical distribution

If we treat the raw data as a density:
$$
\hat f_{\text{emp}}(x) = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^T \delta(x - x_i).
$$

- Each observation is a point mass aka ``spike"
- Graphically: vertical spikes at the observed values
- This is the raw input into KDE 

2. KDE: replace spikes with kernels

Recall that a histogram would smooth the spikes into bins. Instead of bins, the KDE:

- Replaces each spike $\delta(x - x_i)$ with a small smooth bump
- The bump is the kernel, centered at $x_i$


$$
\delta(x - x_i)
\;\longrightarrow\;
\frac{1}{h}K\!\left(\frac{x - x_i}{h}\right)
$$


- Each observation contributes a local density ``hill''
- Shape determined by the kernel $K$
- Width controlled by the bandwidth $h$

3. Build the density curve by stacking bumps

The KDE density curve is simply:
$$
\hat f(x) = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^T
\text{(kernel bump centered at } x_i\text{)}.
$$

Graphically:

- Place one kernel at each data point
- Scale each kernel so its total area equals $1/T$
- Add all kernels together

The resulting density curve is:

- Smooth (if the kernel is smooth)
- Continuous (no bins)
-  Higher in regions where many kernel bumps overlap
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
How simulate from the KDE? 
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}

- Randomly select an observed data point $x_i$ (each with probability $1/T$) 
- Draw noise $\varepsilon$ from the kernel, scaled by the bandwidth 
  - Kernel controls the \pause shape, while Bandwidth controls the  scale 
  - A wider bandwidth stretches the kernel so that noise draws are larger 
  - For consistency we usually use the same bandwidth for simulation as we used for estimation 
- Form a simulated draw:
  $$
  \tilde{x} = x_i + \varepsilon
  $$
:::

### Estimation

For asset $i$, the KDE is:

$$
\widehat f_i(r)=\frac{1}{T h_i}\sum_{t=1}^{T}
K\left(\frac{r-r_{it}}{h_i}\right),
$$

where $K$ is the kernel and $h_i$ is the bandwidth. We use a Gaussian kernel and
the normal-reference bandwidth (`bw.nrd0`) for the main comparison.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
Estimate the bandwidth for each asset within the calibration sample. 
:::

```{r}
#| label: fit-kde

kde_estimates <- calibration |>
  group_by(asset_id) |>
  summarise(
    bw_nrd0 = bw.nrd0(return),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(kde_estimates, digits = 5, caption = "KDE bandwidth estimates")
```
:::

### Simulation

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
How can we use KDE-based simulation to achieve the risk manager's goal?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- Estimate each asset's return density without assuming that it is Gaussian.
- Construct the density by placing a kernel around every calibration return.
- Draw daily returns from the fitted KDE and compound those draws into one-year
  wealth paths.
- Summarize the paths with the same risk measures used for the Gaussian model.
- KDE can reproduce skewness, heavy tails, and mixtures, although the result
  depends importantly on the bandwidth.
:::

With a Gaussian kernel, an exact KDE draw has a transparent smoothed-bootstrap
interpretation:

1. Select a calibration return $r_j$ at random.
2. Draw $\varepsilon\sim N(0,h^2)$.
3. Set $r^{\mathrm{sim}}=r_j+\varepsilon$.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
Focus on Asset 3.  Draw 10 samples via draw_kde using this asset's estimated bandwidth. 
:::

```{r}
#| label: demonstrate-kde-draw

example_id <- "Asset 3"
example_returns <- calibration |>
  filter(asset_id == example_id) |>
  pull(return)
example_bandwidth <- bw.nrd0(example_returns)

set.seed(6503)
example_kde_draws <- draw_kde(
  n = 10,
  x = example_returns,
  bandwidth = example_bandwidth
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
tibble(simulated_return = example_kde_draws) |>
  mutate(simulated_return = percent(simulated_return, accuracy = 0.01)) |>
  kable(caption = paste("Ten illustrative KDE draws for", example_id))
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
How does KDE simulation differ from simply resampling historical returns?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- Ordinary resampling can reproduce only values observed in the calibration
  sample.
- Gaussian-kernel KDE first selects an observation and then adds continuous
  noise controlled by the bandwidth.
- It can therefore generate returns that were not observed exactly, including
  values slightly beyond the historical range.
- KDE remains a model: its kernel, bandwidth, sample, and stationarity
  assumptions all affect its output.
- Because arithmetic returns cannot fall below $-100\%$, the helper function
resamples any such draw. Under the calibrated daily distributions, this event
should be exceptionally rare. The rule is explicit rather than silently clipping
a draw to an arbitrary boundary.
:::

### Bandwidth and the bias–variance tradeoff


::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
Focus on Asset 3.  Construct a plot of the empirical density with bandwidth 0.5. Repeat for 1 and 2. 
:::

```{r}
#| label: bandwidth-adjust
#| output: false

adjust_values <- c(0.5, 1, 2)

bandwidth_curves <- map_dfr(adjust_values, function(adjust_value) {
  estimate <- density(example_returns, bw = "nrd0", adjust = adjust_value,
                      n = 1024)
  tibble(
    return = estimate$x,
    density = estimate$y,
    bandwidth = paste0("adjust = ", adjust_value)
  )
})


ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(
    data = tibble(return = example_returns),
    aes(return, y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 45, fill = "grey85", color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = bandwidth_curves,
    aes(return, density, color = bandwidth),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(
    title = "The KDE changes substantially with bandwidth",
    subtitle = paste("Illustration using", example_id),
    x = "Daily return",
    y = "Density",
    color = NULL
  )

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}
```{r}
#| label: bandwidth-adjust-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(
    data = tibble(return = example_returns),
    aes(return, y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 45, fill = "grey85", color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = bandwidth_curves,
    aes(return, density, color = bandwidth),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(
    title = "The KDE changes substantially with bandwidth",
    subtitle = paste("Illustration using", example_id),
    x = "Daily return",
    y = "Density",
    color = NULL
  )
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
What happens when we decrease or increase the KDE bandwidth?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- A smaller bandwidth produces a more irregular density that follows local
  sample features closely. It can reveal structure, but it can also fit noise.
- A larger bandwidth produces a smoother, lower-variance estimate.
- Excessive smoothing can conceal skewness, tail structure, or mixtures.
- Bandwidth selection therefore illustrates the bias–variance tradeoff.
:::

## GAN model

### GAN Intuition

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
Can you describe the purpose and mechanics of a GAN?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}

A GAN is a different kind of nonparametric simulator than KDE. Rather than
building a density explicitly from the data, it trains two competing neural
networks:

- The **generator** maps a draw of low-dimensional random noise
  $z\sim N(0,I)$ to a simulated return $r^{\mathrm{sim}}=G(z)$.
- The **discriminator** $D(\cdot)$ is trained to output the probability that a
  return it is shown came from the historical sample rather than from the
  generator.
- The generator is trained to fool the discriminator: it is updated to
  increase $D(G(z))$, i.e. to produce returns the discriminator mistakes for
  real ones.
- Training alternates between improving the discriminator at distinguishing
  real from fake, and improving the generator at deceiving the current
  discriminator.
- At convergence (in principle) the generator's output distribution matches
  the historical return distribution closely enough that the discriminator
  cannot do better than guessing.

Unlike KDE, the GAN does not place an explicit kernel around each observation,
and unlike the Gaussian model, it does not assume a parametric family.
However, because training solves a difficult adversarial optimization problem,
a GAN's fit can depend heavily on network size, training length, and even the
random seed used to initialize it.
:::

### Estimation

For each asset we estimate the calibration-period mean $\widehat\mu_i$ and
standard deviation $\widehat\sigma_i$, exactly as in the Gaussian model, and
use them only to standardize returns before training:

$$
\tilde r_{it} = \frac{r_{it}-\widehat\mu_i}{\widehat\sigma_i}.
$$

The generator and discriminator are trained on the standardized returns
$\tilde r_{it}$, and the generator's output is rescaled back to the original
units when simulating.

Both networks are small feedforward networks: the generator takes a
`GAN_Z_DIM`-dimensional noise vector, passes it through two hidden layers with
leaky-ReLU activations, and outputs a single simulated (standardized) return.
The discriminator takes a single return and passes it through hidden layers of
the same sizes before a sigmoid output representing the estimated probability
that the return was historical rather than simulated.

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
What is the role of the number of training epochs?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- One epoch corresponds to one full pass of alternating generator/discriminator
  minibatch updates.
- More epochs give the generator more opportunity to learn finer features of
  the historical return distribution, including higher-order moments such as
  skewness and kurtosis.
- Training a GAN is an adversarial optimization problem, not a convex one:
  more epochs do not guarantee monotonic improvement. Training can also
  become unstable, oscillate, or collapse onto too narrow a range of outputs
  ("mode collapse").
- We use a small network and few training epochs per asset so that this
  document renders quickly. A production use of this method would typically
  require more careful tuning, a larger network, and many more epochs, at the
  cost of a materially longer training time.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
Train a GAN on the calibration-period returns for each asset.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fit-gan

gan_fits <- setNames(vector("list", length(asset_levels)), asset_levels)

for (i in seq_along(asset_levels)) {
  id <- asset_levels[i]
  keras3::set_random_seed(300000 + i)

  gan_fits[[id]] <- train_gan(
    calibration |> filter(asset_id == id) |> pull(return),
    z_dim = GAN_Z_DIM,
    hidden_units = GAN_HIDDEN_UNITS,
    epochs = GAN_EPOCHS,
    batch_size = GAN_BATCH_SIZE,
    learning_rate = GAN_LEARNING_RATE,
    asset_name = id
  )
}

gan_scaling <- tibble(
  asset_id = asset_levels,
  mu = map_dbl(gan_fits, "mu"),
  sd = map_dbl(gan_fits, "sd")
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(gan_scaling, digits = 5,
      caption = "Scaling parameters used to standardize returns before GAN training")
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
If the GAN's scaling step matches an asset's mean and standard deviation, does the GAN reproduce the entire distribution?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- No, and for a different reason than with the Gaussian model. The scaling
  step only fixes the location and scale used as inputs to training; it does
  not constrain what the generator actually learns to output.
- The generator can learn a standardized output distribution whose own mean or
  standard deviation differs from the training data, particularly if training
  has not converged well.
- Any resemblance to the historical skewness, kurtosis, or tail behavior is
  entirely a byproduct of adversarial training, with no explicit mechanism
  enforcing it, unlike KDE's bandwidth-controlled smoothing of observed
  returns.
:::

### Simulation

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
How can we use GAN-based simulation to achieve the risk manager's goal?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- Train a generator network on each asset's calibration-period returns,
  standardized to have zero mean and unit variance.
- Draw many low-dimensional noise vectors, pass them through the trained
  generator, and rescale the output back to the original return units.
- Compound simulated daily returns into one-year wealth paths exactly as with
  the Gaussian and KDE models.
- Summarize the simulated paths using the same quantiles, loss probabilities,
  Value at Risk, and Expected Shortfall measures.
- The GAN is nonparametric in the same broad sense as KDE: no distributional
  family is imposed. It differs from KDE in how it builds the simulator --
  through adversarial training of a neural network rather than through
  explicit kernel smoothing of the data.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
Using the same Asset 3 example as for KDE, draw 10 samples from the fitted GAN.
:::

```{r}
#| label: demonstrate-gan-draw

set.seed(7604)
example_gan_draws <- draw_gan(10, gan_fits[[example_id]])
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
tibble(simulated_return = example_gan_draws) |>
  mutate(simulated_return = percent(simulated_return, accuracy = 0.01)) |>
  kable(caption = paste("Ten illustrative GAN draws for", example_id))
```
:::

### GAN training stability and fit diagnostics

Unlike the Gaussian model (a closed-form fit) or KDE (a deterministic function
of the data and bandwidth), a GAN's fit depends on its random weight
initialization and on the path taken by adversarial training. The same
architecture and number of epochs, applied to the same data, can produce
generators of noticeably different quality depending on the random seed.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
For the Asset 3 GAN, simulate 200 replicate return paths of the same length as
the calibration sample. For each path compute the mean, standard deviation,
skewness, and excess kurtosis, and compare the distribution of each statistic
(across paths) to the single historical calibration value.
:::

```{r}
#| label: gan-path-stats
#| output: false

GAN_DIAGNOSTIC_PATHS <- 200L
gan_path_length <- length(example_returns)

set.seed(260000)
gan_path_matrix <- matrix(
  draw_gan(GAN_DIAGNOSTIC_PATHS * gan_path_length, gan_fits[[example_id]]),
  nrow = GAN_DIAGNOSTIC_PATHS, ncol = gan_path_length
)

gan_path_stats <- tibble(
  path_id = seq_len(GAN_DIAGNOSTIC_PATHS),
  mean = apply(gan_path_matrix, 1, mean),
  sd = apply(gan_path_matrix, 1, sd),
  skewness = apply(gan_path_matrix, 1, sample_skewness),
  excess_kurtosis = apply(gan_path_matrix, 1, sample_excess_kurtosis)
)

gan_historical_stats <- distribution_summary(example_returns) |>
  select(mean, sd, skewness, excess_kurtosis)

gan_path_diff_long <- gan_path_stats |>
  mutate(
    mean = mean - gan_historical_stats$mean,
    sd = sd - gan_historical_stats$sd,
    skewness = skewness - gan_historical_stats$skewness,
    excess_kurtosis = excess_kurtosis - gan_historical_stats$excess_kurtosis
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-path_id, names_to = "statistic", values_to = "value")

ggplot(gan_path_diff_long, aes(statistic, value)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5, trim = TRUE, fill = model_colors[["GAN"]]) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 21, size = 3, fill = "white") +
  labs(
    title = paste("GAN simulated path minus historical statistic,", example_id),
    subtitle = "Each point is one simulated path; width shows the spread across 200 paths",
    y = "Simulated \u2212 historical",
    x = NULL
  )
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}
```{r}
#| label: gan-path-stats-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.5

ggplot(gan_path_diff_long, aes(statistic, value)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5, trim = TRUE, fill = model_colors[["GAN"]]) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 21, size = 3, fill = "white") +
  labs(
    title = paste("GAN simulated path minus historical statistic,", example_id),
    subtitle = "Each point is one simulated path; width shows the spread across 200 paths",
    y = "Simulated \u2212 historical",
    x = NULL
  )
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
Does the GAN do a good job at mimicking Asset 3 returns?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Not at this training budget. Asset 3's calibration returns have mean
$\approx-0.04\%$, standard deviation $\approx1.81\%$, skewness
$\approx-1.83$, and excess kurtosis $\approx8.9$ -- a pronounced left skew and
heavy tails. Averaged across the 200 simulated replicate paths, the fitted
generator instead produces a mean of roughly $+0.8\%$ per day, a standard
deviation of roughly $1.4\%$ (about 22% below historical), a skewness near
$0$, and an excess kurtosis near $0$.

- The GAN gets the order of magnitude of daily volatility roughly right, but
  understates it, and it gets the sign and magnitude of the mean wrong by an
  amount that is large relative to how close to zero the true daily mean is.
- More importantly, it misses the defining shape features of this asset: the
  strong negative skew and heavy left tail are almost entirely absent from
  the simulated paths, which look close to symmetric and only mildly
  non-Gaussian.
- These are exactly the features that let KDE outperform the Gaussian model
  for Asset 3 earlier in this document. KDE reproduces them because every
  draw is tied to an actual historical observation; the GAN has no such
  structural guarantee, and with a small network and few epochs it has not
  learned them.
:::

## In-sample fit

### In-sample fitted densities

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
For each asset, identify the features that the Gaussian model misses and assess
whether the KDE and GAN appear to capture genuine structure or local sampling
noise.
:::

A GAN has no closed-form density, so as an approximate density curve for
plotting we draw a large sample from each asset's trained generator and smooth
it with a KDE -- the same plug-in approach used later for the GAN's validation
log score.

```{r}
#| label: in-sample-density-data
#| output: false

set.seed(240000)

density_comparison <- calibration |>
  group_by(asset_id) |>
  group_modify(~ {
    x <- .x$return
    grid <- seq(min(x) - 0.15 * diff(range(x)),
                max(x) + 0.15 * diff(range(x)), length.out = 800)
    kde_fit <- density(x, bw = "nrd0", from = min(grid), to = max(grid), n = 800)
    gan_sample <- draw_gan(KDE_QUANTILE_DRAWS, gan_fits[[as.character(.y$asset_id)]])
    gan_density <- kde_density_at(grid, gan_sample, bw.nrd0(gan_sample))
    bind_rows(
      tibble(return = grid, density = dnorm(grid, mean(x), sd(x)), model = "Gaussian"),
      tibble(return = kde_fit$x, density = kde_fit$y, model = "KDE"),
      tibble(return = grid, density = gan_density, model = "GAN")
    )
  }) |>
  ungroup()


ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(
    data = calibration,
    aes(return, y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 45, fill = "grey85", color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = density_comparison,
    aes(return, density, color = model),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ asset_id, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_colors[c("Gaussian", "KDE", "GAN")]) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Gaussian, KDE, and GAN fits to calibration returns",
    x = "Daily return",
    y = "Density",
    color = NULL
  )
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}
```{r}
#| label: in-sample-density-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 6

ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(
    data = calibration,
    aes(return, y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 45, fill = "grey85", color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = density_comparison,
    aes(return, density, color = model),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ asset_id, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_colors[c("Gaussian", "KDE", "GAN")]) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Gaussian, KDE, and GAN fits to calibration returns",
    x = "Daily return",
    y = "Density",
    color = NULL
  )
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
Does the closer-looking KDE fit establish that KDE is the better model?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- No. KDE usually fits the calibration sample more closely because it is more
  flexible.
- Some fitted features may be sample-specific and may not recur.
- The validation year provides a better test of whether the additional
  flexibility generalizes.
- The GAN's in-sample fit depends on how well adversarial training converged,
  which is not guaranteed even by construction. A visibly worse in-sample fit
  for the GAN does not necessarily mean it is the worse model out of sample --
  but, unlike KDE, it also is not evidence of superior flexibility; it may
  simply reflect incomplete training.
:::

### Compare simulated one-day returns

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
For each asset, draw a large one-day simulation sample from each fitted model and
compare its distribution with the calibration returns.
:::

```{r}
#| label: one-day-simulation

set.seed(1401)

one_day_comparison <- map_dfr(asset_levels, function(id) {
  historical <- calibration |> filter(asset_id == id) |> pull(return)
  fitted <- fit_marginal_models(historical)

  bind_rows(
    distribution_summary(historical) |> mutate(model = "Historical"),
    distribution_summary(draw_gaussian(ONE_DAY_DRAWS, fitted$mu, fitted$sigma)) |>
      mutate(model = "Gaussian"),
    distribution_summary(draw_kde(ONE_DAY_DRAWS, historical, fitted$bw_nrd0)) |>
      mutate(model = "KDE"),
    distribution_summary(draw_gan(ONE_DAY_DRAWS, gan_fits[[id]])) |>
      mutate(model = "GAN")
  ) |>
    mutate(asset_id = id, .before = 1)
})
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
one_day_comparison |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 5))) |>
  kable(caption = "Historical and simulated one-day return distributions")
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
Why can KDE-simulated volatility be slightly higher than historical volatility?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- A Gaussian-kernel KDE draw equals a sampled historical return plus independent
  Gaussian noise.
- The added noise has variance $h^2$, so the fitted KDE variance is
  approximately the empirical variance plus $h^2$.
- A larger bandwidth therefore smooths the density and increases the variance of
  simulated draws.
- Variance-corrected smoothed bootstraps exist, but we retain the ordinary KDE
  here so that the simulation corresponds directly to the density we fitted.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
Why can the Gaussian model match mean and volatility while producing different tail-risk estimates?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- Mean and standard deviation describe only two aspects of a distribution.
- Tail quantiles also depend on skewness, kurtosis, and other features of the
  distributional shape.
- A Gaussian model imposes its tail shape; KDE estimates a more flexible shape
  from the calibration observations.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
Should we expect the GAN's one-day moments to match the Gaussian model's by construction, the way KDE's roughly do?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- No. KDE's one-day mean and variance are tied closely to the empirical mean
  and variance by construction (plus a small bandwidth-driven variance
  inflation), because every draw is a historical observation plus kernel
  noise.
- The GAN has no such built-in link. Its one-day mean, standard deviation,
  skewness, and kurtosis are whatever the trained generator happens to
  produce, so they can deviate further from the historical values -- more so
  than KDE, and in either direction -- particularly for a small network
  trained for relatively few epochs.
- This is the practical cost of the GAN's added flexibility: it has no
  guardrail analogous to a bandwidth that keeps simulated draws anchored near
  the data.
:::

## Out-of-sample

### Simulate one-year paths

Each path contains 252 simulated daily arithmetic returns. Starting with wealth
of 1, path $p$ for asset $i$ evolves as:

$$
W_{i,p,\tau}=\prod_{s=1}^{\tau}(1+r_{i,p,s}^{\mathrm{sim}}).
$$

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
What does one simulated path represent?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- One path is one model-generated version of the asset's next 252 trading days.
- The paths are alternative future years, not additional assets.
- More paths reduce Monte Carlo noise, but they do not provide more historical
  information or remove model risk.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
Use the custom "simulate_paths" function across our assets for the pre-defined number of paths and simulations.  
:::

```{r}
#| label: simulate-all-paths

path_summaries <- list()
path_results <- list()

for (i in seq_along(asset_levels)) {
  id <- asset_levels[i]
  x <- calibration |> filter(asset_id == id) |> pull(return)
  bandwidth <- bw.nrd0(x)

  for (model_name in c("Gaussian", "KDE", "GAN")) {
    set.seed(500000 + i * 10 + match(model_name, c("Gaussian", "KDE", "GAN")))

    result <- simulate_paths(
      x = x,
      model = model_name,
      n_paths = N_PATHS,
      horizon = SIMULATION_DAYS,
      bandwidth = bandwidth,
      gan_fit = gan_fits[[id]],
      keep_paths = TRUE
    )

    path_summaries[[paste(id, model_name, sep = "__")]] <-
      result$summary |> mutate(asset_id = id, .before = 1)
    path_results[[paste(id, model_name, sep = "__")]] <- result
  }
}

path_summary <- bind_rows(path_summaries) |>
  mutate(asset_id = factor(asset_id, levels = asset_levels))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(
  path_summary,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "One-year simulation summaries by asset and model"
)
```
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
Interpret the median drawdown for these assets. 
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Drawdown measures peak to trough loss. The median is the drawdown across the paths of that asset. 

We see asset 3 has the largest drawdowns, indicating the greatest potential risk
:::


::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
Create a side by side plots of the paths for wealth distributions of the Gaussian and KDE estimators.  
:::

}) |>

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
How should we interpret a central 90% simulation band?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- At each horizon, the band runs from the 5th to the 95th percentile of the
  model-generated wealth distribution.
- It summarizes uncertainty conditional on the fitted model and calibration
  sample.
- It is not a guarantee that the realized path will remain inside the band.
- The bands are pointwise: one path may move inside and outside them over time.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
Why can terminal wealth be skewed even when daily returns are Gaussian?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
- Wealth compounds multiplicatively rather than adding daily returns.
- Gains and losses have asymmetric effects on compounded wealth.
- The product of many $(1+r_t)$ terms is therefore not generally symmetric, even
  when the daily return distribution is symmetric.
:::


### Compare planning outcomes

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}

Compare the Gaussian and KDE models on the planning summaries that matter to
the risk manager:

- downside risk, measured by Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall;
- the probability that terminal wealth falls below its starting value; and
- the typical maximum drawdown.

:::

Starting with wealth equal to 1, define the one-year loss on path $p$ fpr asset $i$ as

$$
L_{i,p}=1-W_{i,p,252}.
$$

A positive value of $L_{i,p}$ represents a loss relative to starting wealth.

The 95% Value at Risk is the 95th percentile of the simulated loss
distribution:

$$
\operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(L_i)
=
q_{0.95}(L_i).
$$

It is the loss threshold exceeded by approximately the worst 5% of simulated
paths. Expected Shortfall is the average loss among those worst 5% of paths:

$$
\operatorname{ES}_{0.95}(L_i)
=
E\left[L_i\mid L_i\geq \operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(L_i)\right].
$$

Expected Shortfall is therefore sensitive not only to how often severe losses
occur, but also to how severe those losses are once they occur.

```{r}
#| label: model-risk-comparison

model_risk_comparison <- path_summary |>
  select(
    asset_id,
    model,
    median_terminal_wealth,
    probability_below_one,
    loss_var_95,
    loss_es_95,
    median_max_drawdown
  ) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("Gaussian", "KDE", "GAN"))) |>
  arrange(asset_id, model)

risk_differences <- model_risk_comparison |>
  select(asset_id, model, loss_var_95, loss_es_95) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = model,
    values_from = c(loss_var_95, loss_es_95)
  ) |>
  transmute(
    asset_id,
    var_kde_minus_gaussian =
      loss_var_95_KDE - loss_var_95_Gaussian,
    es_kde_minus_gaussian =
      loss_es_95_KDE - loss_es_95_Gaussian,
    var_gan_minus_gaussian =
      loss_var_95_GAN - loss_var_95_Gaussian,
    es_gan_minus_gaussian =
      loss_es_95_GAN - loss_es_95_Gaussian
  )
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}

```{r}
#| echo: false

model_risk_comparison |>
  mutate(
    probability_below_one =
      percent(probability_below_one, accuracy = 0.1),
    loss_var_95 =
      percent(loss_var_95, accuracy = 0.1),
    loss_es_95 =
      percent(loss_es_95, accuracy = 0.1),
    median_max_drawdown =
      percent(median_max_drawdown, accuracy = 0.1)
  ) |>
  kable(
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Planning outcomes by asset and model"
  )

risk_differences |>
  mutate(
    var_kde_minus_gaussian =
      percent(var_kde_minus_gaussian, accuracy = 0.1),
    es_kde_minus_gaussian =
      percent(es_kde_minus_gaussian, accuracy = 0.1),
    var_gan_minus_gaussian =
      percent(var_gan_minus_gaussian, accuracy = 0.1),
    es_gan_minus_gaussian =
      percent(es_gan_minus_gaussian, accuracy = 0.1)
  ) |>
  kable(
    caption =
      "KDE and GAN minus Gaussian downside risk; positive values indicate more severe risk than the Gaussian model"
  )
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}

Interpret the planning results. Which assets show the most important
differences between the Gaussian and KDE models?

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}

- **Asset 1 has the largest difference in Value at Risk.** KDE increases the
  estimated 95% loss VaR from approximately 21.6% to 24.3%. Its Expected
  Shortfall also increases by about 2.1 percentage points. This is consistent
  with Asset 1's strong negative skewness, high excess kurtosis, and occasional
  extreme losses.

- **Asset 3 has the largest difference in Expected Shortfall.** The two models
  produce nearly identical VaR estimates, approximately 48.3% and 48.6%, but
  KDE increases Expected Shortfall from approximately 52.9% to 55.6%. This
  suggests that both models identify a similar 5% loss threshold, but KDE
  assigns greater severity to losses beyond that threshold.

- **Asset 2 produces very similar results under both models.** This is
  consistent with its approximately symmetric distribution and relatively
  modest excess kurtosis.

- **Asset 4 illustrates why no single summary is sufficient.** KDE produces
  higher median terminal wealth, a lower probability of ending below starting
  wealth, and a lower median maximum drawdown. At the same time, it produces
  slightly larger VaR and Expected Shortfall estimates. The model changes the
  central planning outcomes and the extreme-tail outcomes in different ways.

- These results do not imply that KDE is always more conservative. The effect
  of model choice depends on the asset and on the risk measure being examined.

- **The GAN's one-year outcomes are dramatically different from, and far less
  plausible than, the Gaussian and KDE outcomes for every asset.** Median
  terminal wealth under the GAN ranges from 14% of starting wealth (Asset 4)
  to 670% of starting wealth (Asset 3), versus a tight 86%-112% range for
  Gaussian and KDE across all four assets. For Assets 1 and 3 the GAN's 95%
  VaR and Expected Shortfall are *negative* -- meaning even its simulated
  worst 5% of years show a gain, not a loss. This traces directly back to the
  one-day comparison above: the GAN's per-day mean return is biased by only a
  few basis points relative to the Gaussian and KDE estimates, but compounding
  that small daily bias over 252 trading days produces an enormous distortion
  in the one-year wealth distribution. A model whose one-day fit looks only
  moderately off can therefore be a poor choice for a planning horizon that
  compounds daily returns.

:::

### Validation

The models were calibrated using the first four years of returns. We now
evaluate them using the subsequent 252 daily returns that were not used during
estimation.

A useful validation strategy should examine more than one statistic.

$\underline{\text{Log Score}}$

The goal is to approximate the unknown density that generates future returns.
Call this unknown density $f_0$. Because $f_0$ is not observable, each fitted
model provides a proxy $\widehat f_m$ for that density.

Suppose $r_t$ is one realized return from the validation period. For a
continuous variable, the probability of observing exactly $r_t$ is zero.
Instead, $\widehat f_m(r_t)$ measures the local concentration of probability
around that realized return.

For model $m$, define the score for observation $r_t$ as

$$
\ell_{m,t}
=
\log\left[\widehat f_m(r_t)\right].
$$

The average validation log score is

$$
\operatorname{LogScore}_m
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{t=1}^{n}
\log\left[\widehat f_m(r_t)\right].
$$

The validation average is an empirical estimate of

$$
E_{R\sim f_0}
\left[
\log\left(\widehat f_m(R)\right)
\right],
$$

the model's expected log density when evaluated at a future return generated
by the unknown process.

Consider a realized validation return of $r_t=-15\%$. Suppose the Gaussian
model assigns essentially no density to returns near $-15\%$:

$$
\widehat f_{\text{Gaussian}}(-0.15)=10^{-12}.
$$

Its score for this observation is therefore

$$
\log(10^{-12})\approx -27.63.
$$

Now suppose the calibration sample contains an extreme loss near $-15\%$.
The KDE places a kernel around that observation and assigns greater local
density to returns near $-15\%$:

$$
\widehat f_{\text{KDE}}(-0.15)=10^{-3}.
$$

The KDE receives the score

$$
\log(10^{-3})\approx -6.91.
$$

Thus, KDE receives a substantially better score for this realized return:

$$
-6.91-(-27.63)=20.72.
$$

The KDE is rewarded because it assigned more density to the region where the
return actually occurred. The Gaussian model is penalized because its fitted
density regarded that outcome as extremely unlikely. The numerical density
values above are illustrative; a density is not itself a probability and need
not lie between zero and one.

The log score repeats this comparison for every validation return. A model can
outperform another model because it assigns more density to important
observations, particularly observations that the competing model regards as
extremely unlikely. However, if KDE places too much density around unusual
calibration observations that do not recur, it may perform worse on the
remaining validation returns.

Higher average log scores are better. The logarithm strongly penalizes a model
when it assigns extremely low density to a realized return, so the score
rewards models that allocate density effectively across the full validation
sample, including its tails.


$\underline{Coverage}$

For a nominal predictive interval
$\left[\widehat q_{\alpha/2},\widehat q_{1-\alpha/2}\right]$, empirical
coverage is

$$
\operatorname{Coverage}_{1-\alpha}
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{t=1}^{n}
\mathbf{1}
\left\{
\widehat q_{\alpha/2}
\leq r_t
\leq
\widehat q_{1-\alpha/2}
\right\}.
$$

For example, a well-calibrated 90% interval should contain approximately 90% of
the validation returns. We examine several interval levels because a model can
have reasonable central coverage while still misrepresenting the tails.


$ \underline{Tail Frequency}$

The realized 5% tail frequency is

$$
\operatorname{TailFrequency}_{0.05}
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{t=1}^{n}
\mathbf{1}
\left\{
r_t\leq \widehat q_{0.05}
\right\}.
$$

This should be compared with 0.05:

- a value above 0.05 suggests that the model underestimates the frequency of
  sufficiently bad returns;
- a value below 0.05 suggests that the model predicts too many bad returns.

Because the validation sample contains only 252 observations, these measures
are subject to sampling variation. The validation evidence should therefore be
interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="false" title="Task"}
Use the custom validation_metrics function on the validation sample for each asset. Produce a table as well as bar chart of the log score for each asset under the Gaussian, KDE, and GAN approaches. 
:::

The GAN has no closed-form density, so `validation_metrics()` treats it the
same way the in-sample density plot did: it draws a large reference sample
from the trained generator and fits a KDE to that sample as a plug-in
approximation to the GAN's implied density. Coverage and tail frequency for
the GAN are based directly on the quantiles of that same reference sample.

```{r}
#| label: validation-metrics

validation_results <- map_dfr(seq_along(asset_levels), function(i) {
  id <- asset_levels[i]

  train_x <- calibration |>
    filter(asset_id == id) |>
    pull(return)

  validation_x <- validation |>
    filter(asset_id == id) |>
    pull(return)

  set.seed(800000 + i)

  validation_metrics(
    train = train_x,
    validation = validation_x,
    bandwidth = bw.nrd0(train_x),
    kde_quantile_draws = KDE_QUANTILE_DRAWS,
    gan_fit = gan_fits[[id]]
  ) |>
    mutate(asset_id = id, .before = 1)
}) |>
  mutate(
    asset_id = factor(asset_id, levels = asset_levels),
    model = factor(model, levels = c("Gaussian", "KDE", "GAN"))
  )
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}

```{r}
#| echo: false

validation_results |>
  mutate(
    coverage_90 = percent(coverage_90, accuracy = 0.1),
    coverage_95 = percent(coverage_95, accuracy = 0.1),
    coverage_98 = percent(coverage_98, accuracy = 0.1),
    predicted_q05 = percent(predicted_q05, accuracy = 0.1),
    realized_below_q05 =
      percent(realized_below_q05, accuracy = 0.1)
  ) |>
  kable(
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Out-of-sample validation by asset and model"
  )
```

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Output"}

```{r}
#| label: validation-log-score-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.5

validation_results |>
  ggplot(aes(asset_id, log_score, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
    width = 0.6
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = model_colors[c("Gaussian", "KDE", "GAN")]
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Out-of-sample log score by asset and model",
    subtitle = "Higher values indicate better predictive density",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Mean validation log score",
    fill = NULL
  )
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}

Interpret the validation results. What do the log scores, coverage measures,
and tail frequencies suggest?

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}

- KDE has a higher validation log score for Assets 1, 3, and 4. For Asset 2,
  the two scores are essentially identical. The Gaussian model is therefore
  adequate for Asset 2, while KDE appears to assign more useful predictive
  density to the validation returns for the other three assets.

- The GAN has the lowest validation log score of the three models for every
  asset, consistent with the one-day and path-simulation comparisons above.
  Its interval coverage is particularly poor for Assets 2 and 4: the nominal
  90% interval covers only about 59% and 62% of validation returns,
  respectively, versus approximately 90% for Gaussian and KDE. Its realized
  5% tail frequency is also elevated for Assets 1-3 (around 7.5%-12.3%,
  versus roughly 5%-7% for Gaussian and KDE), reflecting the underestimated
  volatility documented earlier. This is a direct consequence of the small
  network and short training schedule used here, not an inherent property of
  GAN-based simulation.

- Asset 3 deserves particular attention. Both models realize a 5% tail
  frequency of approximately 6.75%, which is above the nominal 5% level. Both
  models therefore appear to underestimate the frequency of sufficiently bad
  daily returns for this asset.

- The coverage results are generally close to their nominal levels, but they
  are not identical across interval widths. This illustrates why evaluating
  only one predictive interval can conceal model weaknesses.

- Asset 4 has a realized 5% tail frequency below 5% under both models. In this
  validation sample, both models are somewhat conservative with respect to the
  frequency of very negative daily returns.

- The validation evidence does not identify one universally superior model.
  Log score evaluates the overall quality of the predictive density, while
  coverage and tail frequency focus on calibration at selected regions of the
  distribution. These measures provide complementary evidence.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}

Why might KDE fit better in sample but produce a worse validation log score?

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}

- A small bandwidth can cause KDE to adapt closely to idiosyncratic
  calibration-period observations.

- Those local features may reflect sampling noise and may not recur during the
  validation period.

- KDE can therefore have lower bias but higher variance than the Gaussian
  model.

- This is the same bias–variance tradeoff encountered throughout machine
  learning.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}

Across every comparison in this document, how does the GAN's reliability
compare with the Gaussian and KDE models?

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}

Across the in-sample density overlay, the one-day moment comparison, the
one-year path simulations, and the out-of-sample validation metrics, the GAN
as configured here is consistently the least reliable of the three models:
it understates volatility, misses skewness and kurtosis almost entirely for
the heavier-tailed assets, has the lowest validation log score for every
asset, and -- most consequentially -- compounds small daily mean biases into
economically large distortions in one-year planning outcomes.

This is not evidence that GANs are unsuitable for this task in general. It
reflects a deliberate choice, made to keep this document fast to render, to
train a small network for very few epochs. The Gaussian model requires
estimating only two parameters per asset and matches the data by
construction. KDE requires choosing a single bandwidth and is tied directly
to the observed data, so it degrades gracefully. A GAN instead requires
solving a genuinely difficult non-convex adversarial optimization problem
with no such guardrail, and its quality depends on network size, training
length, and random initialization in a way that neither of the other two
models' quality does. A fair comparison with a production-grade GAN would
require considerably more architecture and training-time investment --
and, even then, the comparison would still need the same validation
discipline applied here, since nothing about a GAN's flexibility guarantees
a good fit.

:::
